[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding the Autograd Engine and Computation Graphs in PyTorch"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Deep learning models rely heavily on automatic differentiation to compute gradients efficiently. PyTorch provides a built-in engine called torch.autograd that automates the process of calculating derivatives for tensor operations."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"How Computation Graphs Work"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you perform operations on PyTorch tensors with requires_grad=True, PyTorch dynamically constructs a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) in the background. The leaves of this graph are the input tensors, and the roots are the output tensors."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Forward Pass: The data flows through the network, and the computation graph records every operation performed on tensors."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Backward Pass: Gradients are computed by traversing the graph backward from the root to the leaves using the chain rule."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Practical Implementation"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Let us look at a simple code example demonstrating how to create tensors with gradient tracking and compute their derivatives."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"import torch

x = torch.tensor([2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
y = x * 2 + 3
z = y.sum()
z.backward()
print(x.grad)"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the code above, the output x.grad will return tensor([2., 2.]) because the derivative of z with respect to x is 2 for each element."}]
